name: Rifampicin
mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta subunit, rpoB gene), blocking mRNA synthesis. Bactericidal against M. tuberculosis (intracellular and extracellular). Broad-spectrum: also Staph aureus (including MRSA), Neisseria meningitidis, Legionella. Penetrates tissues/cells well. Resistance develops rapidly if used alone (rpoB mutations) - always use in combination
dosing: TB: <50kg: 450mg daily; ≥50kg: 600mg daily. Give 30-60 min before food or 2h after (food ↓ absorption). Part of 6-month regimen (2 months RIPE, then 4 months RI). Meningitis prophylaxis: 600mg BD for 2 days. MRSA eradication (combination): 600mg BD for 5-10 days. Reduce dose if hepatic impairment (max 8mg/kg if severe). IV if oral not possible (same doses, infuse over 2-3h)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to rifamycins. Jaundice. Concurrent with ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors (complex interaction). Caution: hepatic impairment (monitor closely), alcohol excess, porphyria, renal impairment (reduce dose if severe)
interactions: POTENT CYP450 INDUCER (3A4, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6) - ↓ levels of MANY drugs. CRITICAL: warfarin (↓ INR - increase warfarin dose, monitor closely), hormonal contraceptives (↓ efficacy - USE ADDITIONAL barrier contraception + consider higher-dose estrogen or alternative), antiretrovirals (complex - many interactions, specialist advice), azoles (fluconazole, voriconazole ↓ levels - avoid/dose increase), immunosuppressants (ciclosporin, tacrolimus ↓ levels - increase dose, monitor), phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonylureas, statins, methadone, benzodiazepines, corticosteroids. Isoniazid: additive hepatotoxicity. Alcohol: ↑ hepatotoxicity
monitoring: LFTs baseline, then 2-weekly for 2 months, then monthly (hepatotoxicity common - stop if ALT >5× ULN or symptomatic). Signs of hepatitis (jaundice, N&V, abdominal pain - advise patients report immediately). FBC (thrombocytopenia, anaemia - rarely). Renal function. Culture/sensitivity. Adherence (DOT recommended). Visual acuity if on ethambutol. Drug interactions (review all medications, adjust doses - especially warfarin, contraceptives, immunosuppressants)
pregnancy: USE if indicated - untreated TB greater risk. Rifampicin safe in pregnancy (WHO/NICE recommend). Risk of neonatal haemorrhage (vitamin K deficiency - rifampicin induces metabolism). Give vitamin K to mother in last weeks and to neonate at birth. Monitor for hepatotoxicity
sideEffects: Common: hepatotoxicity (dose-related, transient LFT elevation common, clinical hepatitis 1-2% - RISK FACTORS: pre-existing liver disease, alcohol, concurrent hepatotoxic drugs, first 2 months of therapy), orange/red discoloration of bodily fluids (urine, tears, saliva, sweat - harmless, warn patients, can stain contact lenses), GI upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain). Flu-like syndrome (intermittent dosing - fever, chills, myalgia - more with non-daily regimens). Uncommon: rash, pruritus, thrombocytopenia (immune-mediated, especially intermittent dosing - stop if develops), acute kidney injury (interstitial nephritis), haemolytic anaemia. Rare: severe hypersensitivity, SLE-like syndrome, pseudomembranous colitis
pharmacokinetics: Well absorbed orally (food ↓ absorption - take on empty stomach). Peak 2-4h. Widely distributed, including CSF (inflamed meninges). Undergoes enterohepatic circulation. Autoinduction: induces own metabolism (levels ↓ over first 2 weeks, then stabilize). Half-life: 2-5h. Excreted: bile (60%), urine (30%). Colours secretions orange-red (deacetyl metabolite)
clinicalPearls: CORNERSTONE of TB treatment. Part of standard 6-month regimen (RIPE × 2 months, then RI × 4 months). ESSENTIAL in continuation phase (bactericidal, prevents relapse). RESISTANCE: rpoB mutations. Rapidly develops if used alone - ALWAYS combination therapy. DRUG INTERACTIONS: EXTENSIVE - potent CYP inducer. CHECK ALL medications before starting. KEY INTERACTIONS: warfarin (↓ INR - may need 50-100% warfarin dose increase, INR monitoring 2-3x/week initially), COCP/POP (↓ efficacy - ADDITIONAL barrier contraception throughout and 4-8 weeks after stopping, consider copper IUD or depo medroxyprogesterone), antiretrovirals (complex - avoid certain PIs, adjust efavirenz/nevirapine, specialist advice), immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, ciclosporin levels ↓ significantly - may need 3-5× dose increase, monitor levels), azoles (↓ levels - may need alternative antifungal). HEPATOTOXICITY: common (especially with isoniazid). BLACK BOX: monitor LFTs regularly, educate patients (stop if jaundice, N&V, abdominal pain). Higher risk: pre-existing liver disease, alcohol, hepatitis, HIV, first 2 months. ORANGE DISCOLORATION: warn patients (urine, tears, saliva, semen, sweat turn orange/red). Harmless but alarming if unexpected. Stains contact lenses - remove before taking. TAKE ON EMPTY STOMACH: 30-60 min before food or 2h after (food ↓ absorption 30%). ADHERENCE: essential - poor adherence → resistance. DOT (directly observed therapy) recommended. MENINGOCOCCAL PROPHYLAXIS: rifampicin 600mg BD × 2 days (alternative to ciprofloxacin). MRSA decolonisation: combination with mupirocin nasal oint + chlorhexidine washes. Not monotherapy (resistance). BREASTFEEDING: safe (small amounts in milk, orange discoloration of infant urine). ALTERNATIVES if intolerant: rifabutin (fewer interactions, more expensive), fluoroquinolones (second-line - moxifloxacin, levofloxacin). NEVER without full TB regimen (resistance risk)
indication: Active tuberculosis (pulmonary and extrapulmonary) as part of multi-drug regimen. Latent TB (with isoniazid, 3 months). Meningococcal prophylaxis (close contacts). MRSA eradication (combination therapy). Legionella pneumonia (combination with macrolide). Prosthetic joint infections (Staph - with fluoroquinolone)
